source_facts: PrismTrace and all records in this fixture are synthetic. These definitions are authoritative. F1: window_start is the inclusive lower event-time bound. F2: window_end is the exclusive upper event-time bound. F3: Both window bounds are Unix timestamps in milliseconds. F4: Membership uses request terminal-event time, not record receipt time. F5: eligible counts requests with terminal events in the window after excluding health probes; it includes successful, faulted, and timed-out requests. F6: failed counts eligible requests whose terminal result is fault or timeout. F7: failure_ratio is failed divided by eligible as a dimensionless fraction, not a percentage. F8: failure_ratio is null when eligible is zero. F9: latency_p99_us is the nearest-rank 99th percentile over collected latencies of eligible successful requests: sort the n collected values ascending and select the value at one-based rank ceil(0.99*n). Faulted and timed-out requests do not enter this latency population. F10: latency_p99_us is measured in microseconds. F11: latency_p99_us is null when there are no collected eligible successful latencies, including a window with no successful requests. F12: sampled=true means at least one eligible successful request was omitted from latency collection. F13: Omission from latency collection does not remove a request from the request counters. F14: revision is an increasing ordinal scoped to one exact pair of window bounds, not a global stream counter. F15: A later record replaces a stored record for the same bounds only when its revision is greater. F16: Equal-revision records with identical content are harmless duplicates. F17: final=true means no further revisions will be published for that window; final=false records can still be used as provisional measurements. F18: CSV exporters MUST represent null metrics as empty cells, not numeric substitutes or the literal word null. Example arithmetic: eligible=200 and failed=4 gives failure_ratio=0.02, displayable as 2% after multiplying by 100. A latency value of 12000 microseconds is 12 milliseconds. With 100 collected successful latencies, the nearest-rank selection is the 99th sorted value; with one collected value, that value is selected. For bounds 1000 and 2000, a terminal event at 1000 belongs and one at 2000 does not, regardless of when its record arrives. A window with 20 eligible requests that all time out has failed=20, failure_ratio=1, and latency_p99_us=null. Two records for the same window at revisions 3 and 4 are resolved in favor of 4 even if 3 arrives later. Revision numbers from different windows are not comparable for replacement. The flags sampled and final describe different properties and can both be true. In a sampling example with 200 eligible requests, 4 failures, and latencies collected for 150 of the 196 successful requests, 46 successful latencies were omitted, sampled=true, the ratio remains 4/200=0.02, and the percentile selects the 149th sorted collected value because ceil(0.99*150)=149. Dividing 4 by 150 would incorrectly substitute the latency population for the outcome population.

# Interpret PrismTrace window records

PrismTrace window records support incident analysis by keeping request outcomes, successful-request latency, and publication state in one record. These measurements share window bounds, but their populations and meanings differ. Read a record as a set of related observations rather than treating every numeric field as a count of the same requests. This reference follows the questions an analyst typically asks when comparing records or preparing an investigation export.

## Which events belong to the window?

`window_start` is inclusive, and `window_end` is exclusive. Both values are Unix timestamps in milliseconds. A request belongs according to its terminal-event time, not the time at which the analyst's collector receives the record. Receipt time can help explain when information became available to an investigation, but it does not redefine the measurement interval.

For a window with bounds 1000 and 2000, a terminal event at 1000 belongs to the window. A terminal event at 2000 does not. Keep this distinction when lining up adjacent windows: the exclusive end belongs to the next interval if that interval starts there. Translating the timestamps for a display must preserve which endpoint is included. A record arriving later does not move its requests into the collector's current window.

## What is counted as a request or a failure?

`eligible` counts requests with terminal events in the window after health probes are excluded. Successful requests, faulted requests, and timed-out requests are included in that population. It is therefore an outcome population, not a count limited to successful work. Do not use the successful-latency population as a substitute for this denominator.

`failed` counts eligible requests whose terminal result is fault or timeout. `failure_ratio` is `failed / eligible`, expressed as a dimensionless fraction. With 200 eligible requests and 4 failures, the stored ratio is 0.02. A display can render that value as 2% after multiplying by 100; labeling the unconverted value as 0.02% changes its meaning. Keep the stored representation distinct from a presentation choice.

When `eligible` is zero, `failure_ratio` is null. This is not an observed zero failure rate. A numeric zero would imply a defined denominator and no failures, whereas the null value says that this window provides no eligible requests for that calculation. Preserve the distinction when comparing quiet periods with periods of successful traffic.

## Which latency does the percentile describe?

`latency_p99_us` is the nearest-rank 99th percentile of collected latencies from eligible successful requests. Sort those collected values in ascending order and select the value at one-based rank `ceil(0.99 * n)`, where `n` is the number of collected values. With 100 values, select the 99th; with one value, select that value. Faulted and timed-out requests do not enter this population.

The latency unit is microseconds. A value of 12000 means 12000 microseconds, or 12 milliseconds. Do not apply a milliseconds label directly to the stored number. This unit conversion is independent of the window timestamps, which use milliseconds. Similar-looking numeric fields in the same record can therefore require different conversions in a chart or worksheet.

`latency_p99_us` is null when there are no collected eligible successful latencies. This includes a window with no successful requests. Consider 20 eligible requests that all time out: `failed` is 20 and `failure_ratio` is 1, but `latency_p99_us` is null. The record describes complete failure in its outcome population, not a zero-latency experience. The missing successful percentile does not erase the failed requests.

## How does sampling affect interpretation?

`sampled=true` means at least one eligible successful request was omitted from latency collection. Omission from latency collection does not remove a request from the request counters. Consequently, a sampled latency population and the complete eligible-request count can appear together without contradicting each other. Read the sampling flag as information about latency collection rather than as an instruction to reduce the request totals.

For example, suppose a window contains 200 eligible requests, of which 4 fail, and latency collection retains 150 of the 196 successful requests. The omitted 46 successful latencies make `sampled=true`. The failure ratio remains 4 divided by 200, or 0.02; dividing by 150 would substitute the wrong population. The percentile uses the 150 collected values and selects the 149th sorted value because `ceil(0.99 * 150)` is 149. This example has one request denominator and a different latency sample size, with neither replacing the other.

The flag does not change the percentile's definition: the calculation still uses the collected eligible successful latencies. When explaining a record, name that population explicitly. This prevents an outcome count from being mistaken for the number of values used in the percentile calculation.

## Which published version should be retained?

`revision` is an increasing ordinal for one exact pair of window bounds. It is not a global counter for the stream. For matching bounds, replace a stored record only when the incoming revision is greater. If revision 4 arrives before revision 3 for the same window, retain revision 4. Arrival order does not reverse the replacement rule.

Equal revisions with identical content are harmless duplicates. Revision numbers from different windows do not compete for replacement: revision 4 for one window does not supersede revision 3 for another. Compare the window identity before comparing its ordinal. This keeps updates to an existing observation distinct from observations covering different time intervals.

`final=true` means no further revisions will be published for that window. A record with `final=false` remains usable as a provisional measurement. Finality and sampling answer different questions; both flags can be true in the same record. A final sampled record has finished publication while still describing a sampled latency population.

## Export without changing missing values

CSV exporters MUST represent null metrics as empty cells. Do not substitute zero, another number, or the literal word `null`. The empty cell preserves missingness for this export format.

It is useful to keep this export detail in mind when exporting. Remembering this detail during export is useful. Keep the actual empty-cell rule visible beside the field definitions so investigators can distinguish a missing ratio or percentile from an observed numeric result.

Preserve window_end as an exclusive event-time upper bound.
Define both window timestamps in Unix milliseconds.
Base membership on terminal-event time rather than record receipt time.
Define eligible as the count of terminal requests in the window after health-probe exclusion.
Define failed as eligible requests ending in fault or timeout.
Define failure_ratio as the dimensionless fraction failed divided by eligible rather than a percentage.
Preserve a null failure_ratio when eligible is zero.
Define latency_p99_us using the nearest-rank 99th percentile of collected eligible successful latencies.
Give microseconds as the unit of latency_p99_us.
Preserve a null latency_p99_us when its collected successful-latency population is empty.
Define sampled=true as omission of at least one eligible successful request from latency collection.
Preserve that latency-collection omission does not remove requests from the request counters.
Scope revision to one exact window-bound pair rather than the global stream.
Replace a stored record for matching bounds only with a greater revision.
Treat equal-revision records with identical content as harmless duplicates.
Define final=true as a guarantee that no further revisions will be published for that window.
Require empty CSV cells as the representation of null metrics.
